# Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking

ShengYun Peng Affiliation: Meta Superintelligence Labs
Affiliation: Georgia Tech Work done at Meta    Pin-Yu Chen
Affiliation: IBM Research    Eric Smith Affiliation: Meta
Superintelligence Labs    Song Jiang Affiliation: Meta Superintelligence

Wang Affiliation: Meta Superintelligence Labs Work done at Meta   
Mahesh Pasupuleti Affiliation: Meta Superintelligence Labs    Duen Horng
Chau Affiliation: Georgia Tech    Jianfeng Chi Affiliation: Meta
Superintelligence Labs Work done at Meta

###### Abstract

\Acp

lrm “think” by generating structured cot (cot) before producing a final
answer, yet they still lack the ability to reason critically about
safety alignment and are easily biased when a flawed premise is injected
into their thought process. We propose RECAP (Robust Safety Alignment
via Counter-Aligned Prefilling), a principled rl (rl) method for
post-training that explicitly teaches models to override flawed
reasoning trajectories and reroute to safe and helpful responses. RECAP
trains on a mixture of synthetically generated counter-aligned cot
prefills and standard prompts, integrates seamlessly into standard rlhf
(rlhf) pipelines without additional rl optimization steps or
architectural modifications, and substantially improves safety and
jailbreak robustness, reduces overrefusal, and preserves core reasoning
capability — all while maintaining inference token budget. Extensive
analysis shows that RECAP-trained models engage in self-reflection more
frequently and remain robust under adaptive attacks, preserving safety
even after repeated attempts to override their reasoning.  
This paper includes potentially offensive red-teaming data and
model-generated content.

## 1 Introduction

Frontier lrm, such as DeepSeek-R1 ([Guo et al., 2025](#bib.bib9)),
OpenAI-o3 ([OpenAI,](#bib.bib26) ), and Qwen3 ([Team,
2025](#bib.bib37)), have achieved remarkable performance in math ([Shao
et al., 2024](#bib.bib35)) and coding ([Jiang et al.,
2024a](#bib.bib17)) tasks, where they “think” by first generating
structured cot reasoning before producing a final answer ([Zhang et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib43); [Xu et al., 2025](#bib.bib41)). Trained via online
RL algorithms, such as grpo (grpo) ([Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib35)),
lrm exhibit emergent behaviors such as “aha moments,” where the model
revisits earlier steps or backtracks to refine its reasoning ([Guo
et al., 2025](#bib.bib9); [Zhou et al., 2025a](#bib.bib48); [Xie et al.,
2025](#bib.bib40)). Yet recent work shows that prefilling the cot with a
simple phrase like “I know that” can bypass alignment constraints and
elicit unsafe completions ([Rager et al., 2025](#bib.bib32)), raising
concerns about whether lrm truly understand how to reason safely ([Huang
et al., 2025a](#bib.bib10); [Chen et al., 2025](#bib.bib5)). Since cot
prefilling is widely supported in both open-source models ([Jeung
et al., 2025](#bib.bib14)) and commercial APIs ([Anthropic,
2025](#bib.bib1)), this brittleness highlights a deeper issue: frontier
lrm still lack the ability to reason critically about safety alignment,
as they are easily biased when a flawed premise is injected into their
thought process.

We investigate the root cause of this issue
(Sec. [2](#S2 "2 Following Without Thinking: The Brittleness of Reasoning in LRMs ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking"))
and discover that once an lrm begins from a flawed cot, it follows
unsafe reasoning into harmful completions and fails to recover from
flawed reasoning. In contrast, prefilling the same lrm with reasoning
traces from a safer model consistently improves its performance. These
findings reveal a generalization gap: during online rl training, models
are commonly rewarded only for correct final responses, while at
inference they have to navigate through noisy reasoning trajectories
that may begin with flawed or misleading steps. This raises a central
question: How can we train lrm to achieve robust safety alignment by
recovering from misleading reasoning, rather than hoping self-correction
will emerge implicitly? To address this gap, we introduce an rl training
recipe that improves safety, reduces overrefusal, and preserves core
reasoning capability, making the following three main contributions
(Fig. [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking")):

![Refer to caption](2510.00938v3/figures/fig1.png)

Figure 1: RECAP trains lrm on a mixture of counter-aligned prefilled and
standard prompts. Harmful prompts are prefilled with unsafe reasoning,
and benign prompts with refusal reasoning, forcing the model to override
flawed trajectories to achieve high rewards. This simple recipe teaches
models to internalize safety values and remain robust under both clean
and adversarial reasoning traces, without modifying standard rlhf
pipelines.

1.  1.  We propose RECAP (Robust Safety Alignment via Counter-Aligned
        Prefilling), a principled rl method for post-training that addresses
        the core brittleness of lrm safety alignment by explicitly training
        models to recover from flawed reasoning traces
        (Sec. [3](#S3 "3 RECAP: Robust Safety Alignment via Counter-Aligned Prefilling ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking")).
        We construct counter-aligned flawed reasoning by prefilling the cot
        of an lrm, inducing it to “think unsafe” for harmful queries and
        “think overly conservative” for benign ones. Naively following these
        prefills would cause the model to provide unsafe instructions or
        overrefuse benign queries. To achieve high rewards, the model must
        instead override these flawed trajectories and recover appropriate
        reasoning. RECAP trains on a mixture of counter-aligned reasoning
        prefills and standard prompts, ensuring that models internalize core
        safety values and can robustly initiate reasoning from both correct
        and flawed traces. RECAP is easy to adopt, requiring no additional
        rl optimization steps or pipeline modifications.
2.  2.  RECAP simultaneously strengthens safety and helpfulness while
        preserving core reasoning capability
        (Sec. [4](#S4 "4 Experiments ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking")).
        In a realistic post-training rl setting with multiple reward
        signals, RECAP delivers substantial gains over vanilla dapo
        (dapo) ([Yu et al., 2026](#bib.bib42)) on DeepSeek-distilled
        Llama-8B and Qwen-14B. Specifically, it achieves on average +12.3%
        on direct harmful benchmarks, +21.0% on jailbreaking benchmarks, and
        +7.8% on the helpfulness score for overrefusal. Crucially, these
        robustness gains generalize to _both_ prefilled and non-prefilled
        prompts at inference time, demonstrating that training with
        counter-aligned reasoning improves safety beyond in-distribution
        prefilling scenarios. At the same time, RECAP preserves mathematical
        reasoning performance on MATH, GSM8K, and AIME2024, despite applying
        no cot prefilling to math prompts during training. Finally, compared
        to vanilla rlhf, RECAP maintains a similar inference-time token
        budget while generating more structured and logically coherent
        reasoning traces.
3.  3.  We demonstrate that RECAP yields persistent robustness even under
        adaptive attacks and fundamentally improves lrm reasoning dynamics
        by increasing the frequency of self-reflection
        (Sec. [5](#S5 "5 Understanding and Stress-Testing RECAP’s Robustness ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking")).
        To stress-test the reasoning safety behavior, we introduce two
        adaptive attacks: full cot hijacking and ipr (ipr), explicitly
        designed to bypass RECAP’s self-reflection mechanism. We find that
        RECAP remains robust against both attacks, preserving safety even
        after repeated attempts to override its reasoning. These robustness
        gains further generalize across prefill-generator model families and
        to unseen code-disguised, semantically rewritten, and
        gradient-optimized jailbreak attacks. A deeper analysis shows that
        RECAP-trained lrm engage in self-reflection more often than vanilla
        rlhf, frequently revising unsafe or mistaken reasoning
        mid-trajectory. Finally, our ablations reveal that counter-aligned
        prefills are essential to induce self-reflection, and that the ratio
        and length of prefills control the trade-off between safety and
        overrefusal.

## 2 Following Without Thinking: The Brittleness of Reasoning in LRMs

rlhf-tuned lrm exhibit emergent behaviors such as “aha moments,” where
the model allocates more reasoning budget to a problem by revisiting its
initial thought, reflecting on flawed reasoning, and sometimes even
backtracking to reconsider earlier steps ([Guo et al.,
2025](#bib.bib9)). Yet we find that lrm remain highly sensitive to their
initial reasoning direction: when seeded with a misleading cot, they
frequently continue along the flawed trajectory and produce incorrect
outputs; conversely, when provided with a higher-quality reasoning trace
than they could generate on their own, they tend to follow it to a
better answer. To understand this phenomenon,
Sec. [2.1](#S2.SS1 "2.1 Preliminaries ‣ 2 Following Without Thinking: The Brittleness of Reasoning in LRMs ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking")
constructs a suite of controlled case studies, and
Sec. [2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Prefilled Reasoning Traces Steer LRM Behavior Dramatically ‣ 2 Following Without Thinking: The Brittleness of Reasoning in LRMs ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking")
demonstrates how prefilling with different cot traces can dramatically
alter the model’s final response.

|                                                  |             |           |            |            |            |          |
| ------------------------------------------------ | ----------- | --------- | ---------- | ---------- | ---------- | -------- |
|                                                  | DSQwen-1.5B | DSQwen-7B | DSLlama-8B | DSQwen-14B | DSQwen-32B | Qwen3-4B |
| Original                                         | 14.01       | 35.94     | 57.83      | 67.75      | 72.20      | 95.21    |
| $`y^{\text{pre}}_{\text{cot}}`$ from DSQwen-1.5B | 13.31       | 20.77     | 45.05      | 47.59      | 35.14      | 76.68    |
| $`y^{\text{pre}}_{\text{cot}}`$ from DSQwen-32B  | 51.12       | 63.58     | 71.24      | 69.33      | 74.44      | 84.35    |

Table 1: Prefilled reasoning traces steer lrm behavior dramatically.
Prefilling with $`y^{\text{pre}}_{\text{cot}}`$ from DSQwen-1.5B reduces
average safety scores by 36.4%, whereas prefilling with
$`y^{\text{pre}}_{\text{cot}}`$ from DSQwen-32B increases them by 91.7%.
This brittleness extends across model families: Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507,
trained with a different dataset and recipe than the DS models, also
suffers large safety drops when initialized with unsafe cot.
“$`y^{\text{pre}}_{\text{cot}}`$ from DSQwen-1.5B” and
“$`y^{\text{pre}}_{\text{cot}}`$ from DSQwen-32B” denote evaluation
where the first 200 words of cot from the specified model are injected
into the reasoning trace.

### 2.1 Preliminaries

Notation. Let $`\pi_{\theta}`$ denote an lrm parameterized by weights
$`\theta`$. Given an input prompt $`x`$, we represent the model’s output
as $`y=(y_{\text{cot}},y_{\text{resp}})`$, where $`y_{\text{cot}}`$ is
the intermediate cot reasoning and $`y_{\text{resp}}`$ is the final
response. To study reasoning brittleness, we construct prefilling
samples by injecting a partial, pre-generated reasoning trace
$`y^{\text{pre}}_{\text{cot}}`$ into the cot, where
$`y^{\text{pre}}_{\text{cot}}`$ is syntactically fluent but semantically
flawed or counter-aligned. At inference time, the model is given
$`(x,y^{\text{pre}}_{\text{cot}})`$ as input and asked to generate the
continuation $`y^{\text{gen}}_{\text{cot}}`$ followed by
$`y_{\text{resp}}`$. The full output is thus:
$`y=(y^{\text{pre}}_{\text{cot}}\;\|\;y^{\text{gen}}_{\text{cot}},\;y_{\text{resp}})`$,
where $`\|`$ denotes sequence concatenation. This setup allows us to
measure how different types of reasoning prefills affect the final model
behavior.

Evaluation and metrics. We evaluate the safety alignment following the
protocol introduced by [Peng et al. (2025)](#bib.bib30). Specifically,
models are tested on the StrongREJECT benchmark, which contains 313
harmful prompts ([Souly et al., 2024](#bib.bib36)). The model’s final
response $`y_{\text{resp}}`$ is judged by GPT-4o to determine whether it
is safe. Our metric is the safety score, defined as the percentage of
completions judged safe. We report results on DeepSeek-distilled lrm
(abbreviated as DS) ([Guo et al., 2025](#bib.bib9)) and on
Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 reasoning models ([Team, 2025](#bib.bib37)).

### 2.2 Prefilled Reasoning Traces Steer LRM Behavior Dramatically

\Acp

lrm are highly sensitive to their initial reasoning direction. We
hypothesize that the safety of the final response $`y_{\text{resp}}`$
depends strongly on the quality of the intermediate reasoning
$`y_{\text{cot}}`$. To test this, we ask: What happens if a model is
forced to continue from another model’s reasoning trace? We evaluate the
original DS models and observe, as shown in
Table [1](#S2.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 2 Following Without Thinking: The Brittleness of Reasoning in LRMs ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking")
(Original), that larger models generally achieve higher safety scores.
Next, we extract the first 200 words of $`y_{\text{cot}}`$ from the
least safe model, DSQwen-1.5B, and use it as
$`y^{\text{pre}}_{\text{cot}}`$. When the other four DS models are
required to continue from this unsafe prefix, their average safety score
drops by 36.4%
(Table [1](#S2.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 2 Following Without Thinking: The Brittleness of Reasoning in LRMs ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking"),
$`y^{\text{pre}}_{\text{cot}}`$ from DSQwen-1.5B). Conversely, when we
prefill them with the first 200 words of $`y_{\text{cot}}`$ from the
safest model, DSQwen-32B, their safety score increases by 91.7%
(Table [1](#S2.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 2 Following Without Thinking: The Brittleness of Reasoning in LRMs ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking"),
$`y^{\text{pre}}_{\text{cot}}`$ from DSQwen-32B).

The brittleness of reasoning extends across model families. This
sensitivity to initial reasoning direction is not limited to models
within the same family. We test Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507, a reasoning
model from the Qwen 3.0 family trained with a different dataset and
recipe than the DSQwen models (which are finetuned from Qwen 2.5).
Although Qwen3-4B achieves relatively high safety scores under standard
evaluation (no prefill), its performance drops by 19.5% when initialized
with the $`y^{\text{pre}}_{\text{cot}}`$ from DSQwen-1.5B and by 11.4%
when initialized with the $`y^{\text{pre}}_{\text{cot}}`$ from
DSQwen-32B.

Brittleness generalizes beyond safety. In
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B The brittleness of LRMs generalizes beyond safety ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking"),
we extend this analysis to overrefusal and mathematical reasoning tasks.
We observe the same pattern: when prefilled with flawed cot, models are
more likely to produce overcautious refusals or incorrect math
solutions. This indicates that the brittleness revealed in safety
alignment reflects a broader vulnerability in lrm reasoning.

## 3 RECAP: Robust Safety Alignment via Counter-Aligned Prefilling

Building on our finding in
Sec. [2](#S2 "2 Following Without Thinking: The Brittleness of Reasoning in LRMs ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking")
that lrm are easily biased by flawed premises injected into their cot,
we now explore the counter-aligned setting: what if such flawed
reasoning were deliberately introduced during rollouts in online rl, and
the model were trained to recover from it? In other words, can
systematic exposure to counter-aligned reasoning trajectories during
training strengthen safety alignment? In
Sec. [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Constructing Counter-Aligned Prefills ‣ 3 RECAP: Robust Safety Alignment via Counter-Aligned Prefilling ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking"),
we demonstrate how to construct counter-aligned prefills and integrate
them into the rlhf training objective, using dapo as an example.

### 3.1 Constructing Counter-Aligned Prefills

For each training example with prompt $`x`$, we construct a prefilled
cot prefix $`y^{\text{pre}}_{\text{cot}}`$ of length
$`\ell_{\text{pre}}`$, and allow the model to generate a continuation
$`y^{\text{gen}}_{\text{cot}}`$ followed by the final response
$`y_{\text{resp}}`$. We deliberately construct counter-aligned flawed
reasoning by prefilling the cot of an lrm with syntactically fluent yet
semantically misaligned traces, inducing it to “think unsafe” for
harmful queries and “think overly conservative” for benign ones. These
flawed reasoning traces are sampled from external models whose behaviors
are misaligned with the target safety alignment:

- •
  For harmful prompts, $`y^{\text{pre}}_{\text{cot}}`$ is sampled from a
  weakly safety-aligned or helpful-only model $`\pi_{\text{harm}}`$ that
  produces unsafe reasoning.
- •
  For benign prompts, $`y^{\text{pre}}_{\text{cot}}`$ is sampled from an
  overly conservative model $`\pi_{\text{refuse}}`$ that tends to reject
  all inputs including benign ones.

Naively following $`y^{\text{pre}}_{\text{cot}}`$ would cause the model
to produce unsafe instructions or to overrefuse benign prompts. To
obtain high rewards, the model must instead override these flawed
trajectories with $`y^{\text{gen}}_{\text{cot}}`$ and generate an
aligned final response $`y_{\text{resp}}`$. The scalar reward is
assigned based on $`(x,y_{\text{resp}})`$, with the specific reward
designs detailed in
Sec. [4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Evaluation Setups ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking").

We apply this prefilling strategy to a fraction $`\alpha\in(0,1)`$ of
the training dataset $`\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}`$, forming a modified
subset:

|     |                                                                                                                                                                       |     |
| --- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{\text{prefill}}=\{\,x_{i}\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}\mid\Pr(\text{augment }x_{i}\text{ with }y^{\text{pre}}_{\text{cot}})=\alpha\,\}.`$ |     |

Training with prefilled rollouts. We adopt the dapo framework ([Yu
et al., 2026](#bib.bib42)), an enhanced variant of grpo ([Shao et al.,
2024](#bib.bib35)), and extend it to handle prefilled cot. When a prompt
is prefilled, the importance sampling ratio and advantage normalization
are computed only for tokens after the injected prefix
($`t>\ell_{\text{pre}}`$). The training objective is defined over
prompts $`x\sim\mathcal{D}_{\text{prefill}}`$ and groups of rollouts
$`\{o_{i}\}_{i=1}^{G}`$ sampled from the old policy
$`\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(\cdot\mid x)`$:

|                                                                                                                                                     |                                                                                                                                                                                      |                                                 |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------- | ------ | ------------------------------------------- |
|                                                                                                                                                     | $`\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \mathcal{J}_{\text{RECAP}}(\theta)&=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}_{\text{prefill}},\;\{o_{i}\}_{i=1}^{G}\sim\pi_{\theta\_{\text{old}}}(\cdot\mid x)}\\ |
| &\quad\Bigg[\frac{1}{\sum\_{i=1}^{G}                                                                                                                | o\_{i}                                                                                                                                                                               | _{\text{opt}}}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\sum*{t=t*{0}(x)}^{ | o\_{i} | }\min\Big(r*{i,t}(\theta)\,\hat{A}*{i,t},\\ |
| &\qquad\qquad\mathrm{clip}\big(r*{i,t}(\theta),1-\varepsilon*{\text{low}},1+\varepsilon*{\text{high}}\big)\,\hat{A}*{i,t}\Big)\Bigg]\end{aligned}`$ |                                                                                                                                                                                      |

|     |                                      |                                   |
| --- | ------------------------------------ | --------------------------------- | --------------------------- | ------------------------------ | ----- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\text{s.t.}\quad\bigl | \{\,o*{i}\mid R*{i}>\tau\,\}\bigr | <G\quad\text{and}\quad\bigl | \{\,o*{i}\mid R*{i}=0\,\}\bigr | <G.`$ |     |

where

[TABLE]

Here:

- •
  $`R_{i}`$ is the scalar reward assigned to rollout $`o_{i}`$ based on
  $`(x,y_{\text{resp}})`$.
- •
  $`\hat{A}_{i,t}`$ is the normalized advantage estimated over
  $`\{o_{i}\}_{i=1}^{G}`$.
- •
  $`t_{0}(x)=1`$ if $`x`$ is not prefilled, and
  $`t_{0}(x)=\ell_{\text{pre}}+1`$ otherwise.
- •
  $`|o_{i}|`$ is the length of rollout $`o_{i}`$, and
  $`|o_{i}|_{\text{opt}}=|o_{i}|-(t_{0}(x)-1)`$ is the number of
  optimized tokens.
- •
  As in dapo, $`\varepsilon_{\text{low}}`$ and
  $`\varepsilon_{\text{high}}`$ are clipping thresholds, and
  $`r_{i,t}(\theta)`$ is the importance sampling ratio.
- •
  $`\tau`$ is a reward threshold used in dynamic sampling: prompts are
  discarded if all rollouts are bad ($`R_{i}=0`$) or uniformly good
  ($`R_{i}>\tau`$).

RECAP does not require cot exposure at inference time. Counter-aligned
prefilling is used only during training to shape recovery behavior,
which transfers to standard, non-prefilled inputs at deployment
(Sec. [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 RECAP Supports Alignment-Capability Co-Training While Strengthening Robustness ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking")).

## 4 Experiments

We evaluate RECAP in a realistic post-training rl setting where multiple
reward signals are jointly optimized.
Sec. [4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Evaluation Setups ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking")
details the experimental setup, including tasks, datasets, models, and
evaluation metrics.
Sec. [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 RECAP Supports Alignment-Capability Co-Training While Strengthening Robustness ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking")
reports the main results and comparisons against existing alignment and
post-training methods.
Sec. [4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 RECAP Encourages Structured Reasoning Without Increasing Inference-Time Cost ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking")
examines inference-time efficiency, showing that RECAP preserves the
token budget as standard training while producing more structured and
logically coherent reasoning.
Appendix [F](#A6 "Appendix F RECAP generalizes across reward designs and policy optimization algorithms ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking")
demonstrates that RECAP generalizes across reward designs and policy
optimizations.

### 4.1 Evaluation Setups

Benchmarks. We evaluate RECAP across three domains: safety, overrefusal,
and mathematical reasoning. For safety, we consider two types of
prompts: (a) direct harmful prompts, which contain explicitly harmful
instructions, and (b) jailbreaking prompts, which conceal harmful intent
through roleplay or adversarial phrasing. Full benchmark descriptions
are provided in
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Details of evaluation setups ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking").

Models. We use DSLlama-8B and DSQwen-14B, two DeepSeek-distilled
lrm ([Guo et al., 2025](#bib.bib9)), as policy models. These models are
known to have strong reasoning ability but limited safety
alignment ([Knight et al., 2025](#bib.bib19); [Jiang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib16); [Wang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib39)), making them
suitable for testing whether RECAP improves safety without harming
capabilities. Full reward designs and training hyperparameters are
provided in
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Training details and hyperparameters ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking").

### 4.2 RECAP Supports Alignment-Capability Co-Training While Strengthening Robustness

We evaluate RECAP in a joint training setup spanning both alignment and
reasoning capability tasks. The training corpus contains 5K prompts: 1K
harmful prompts from BeaverTails ([Ji et al., 2023](#bib.bib15)), 1K
overrefusal prompts from STAR-1 ([Wang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib39)), and
3K math prompts from GSM8K ([Cobbe et al., 2021](#bib.bib6)) and
MATH ([Lightman et al., 2023](#bib.bib24)). Results for DSLlama-8B and
DSQwen-14B are reported in
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.2 RECAP Supports Alignment-Capability Co-Training While Strengthening Robustness ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking").
RECAP is trained using counter-aligned prefills from DSQwen-7B, while
all robustness evaluations use distinct prefilling sources.

Baselines. We compare RECAP against both alignment-specific and standard
post-training approaches. Alignment-focused baselines include
SafeChain ([Jiang et al., 2025](#bib.bib16)) and STAR ([Wang et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib39)), which construct reasoning-aligned datasets and
apply sft (sft) to improve safety and reduce overrefusal. We also
include sft and dapo baselines trained on the same dataset as RECAP,
ensuring fair comparison.

RECAP substantially improves safety on both direct harmful and jailbreak
prompts. Our method achieves significant gains across all safety
benchmarks. On StrongREJECT, RECAP improves safety scores by over 3%
compared to all other baselines, and by 24% in the harder setting where
harmful cot is prefilled. On jailbreaking benchmarks, RECAP yields
strong improvements compared to vanilla dapo, despite no prefilling
being applied at inference time. This shows that training with
counter-aligned reasoning traces generalizes to jailbreak scenarios,
where prompts are explicitly designed to push the model into unsafe
reasoning. Notably, the harmful prefilling traces used during training
were extracted from DSQwen-7B, a model distinct from both the training
and evaluation policies, underscoring the robustness of the learned
alignment behavior.

RECAP reduces overrefusal while improving safety. A common drawback of
safety alignment is increased overrefusal, where benign inputs are
unnecessarily rejected. In contrast, RECAP improves both safety and
helpfulness. To construct counter-aligned traces for overrefusal, we
first sft DSQwen-7B on the STAR-1 safety-only subset, which primarily
contains harmful prompts and rule-following cot that often lead to
refusals. We then apply this tuned model to the overrefusal dataset and
extract its refusal-oriented reasoning traces as
$`y^{\text{pre}}_{\text{cot}}`$. These traces are used for prefilling
during training, encouraging the model to override initial refusals and
produce helpful responses instead. As shown in
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.2 RECAP Supports Alignment-Capability Co-Training While Strengthening Robustness ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking"),
methods trained solely on safety data (_e.g_., STAR, SafeChain) improve
safety but reduce helpfulness on the overrefusal benchmark. By contrast,
RECAP improves both metrics simultaneously relative to the original
model, which already has a relatively high helpfulness score compared to
other baselines.

Training with RECAP preserves math reasoning capability as standard
rlhf. A natural concern is whether alignment training, especially with
cot prefilling, might degrade other core capabilities such as math.
However, RECAP outperforms standard sft and dapo on MATH and GSM8K,
while maintaining performance on AIME2024. Crucially, no cot prefilling
is applied to math prompts during training; the observed gains emerge
purely from the alignment-oriented prefilling strategy. This indicates
that RECAP not only strengthens safety and helpfulness but also
preserves core reasoning skills. To ensure that this observation is not
an artifact of random initialization or training noise, we repeat these
experiments with multiple random seeds and report mean performance with
standard deviations in
Appendix [I](#A9 "Appendix I Additional Results on Math Reasoning Stability ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking").

### 4.3 RECAP Encourages Structured Reasoning Without Increasing Inference-Time Cost

A potential concern with RECAP is that encouraging reflection and
rerouting during training may lead to longer completions at inference
time, increasing latency and cost. To examine this, we measure the
average number of generated tokens per completion, broken down into cot
tokens ($`y_{\text{cot}}`$) and final response tokens
($`y_{\text{resp}}`$).

Fig. [2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 4.3 RECAP Encourages Structured Reasoning Without Increasing Inference-Time Cost ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking")
compares DSQwen-14B trained with vanilla dapo and with RECAP across
safety, overrefusal, and math domains. Overall, RECAP maintains a
comparable total token budget to vanilla dapo, while achieving the
substantial alignment and capability gains reported in
Sec. [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 RECAP Supports Alignment-Capability Co-Training While Strengthening Robustness ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking").
We observe slightly longer cot traces in safety and overrefusal
settings, and shorter reasoning in math.

Qualitative inspection of generated reasoning further shows that models
trained with RECAP produce more structured, multi-faceted, and logically
connected cot compared to those trained with vanilla dapo. We
hypothesize that this stems from exposing the model to flawed reasoning
during training, which encourages it to explore and resolve more diverse
reasoning paths, patterns it would be unlikely to encounter when
sampling purely from its own policy. Illustrative comparisons are
provided in
Appendix [J](#A10 "Appendix J RECAP encourages structured reasoning without increasing inference-time cost ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking").
These findings suggest that RECAP improves alignment and reasoning
quality without increasing inference-time cost, making it a practical
solution for real-world deployment.

Figure 2: Average number of tokens generated at inference for DSQwen-14B
under RECAP _vs_. dapo across safety, overrefusal, and math benchmarks.
RECAP maintains a comparable total token budget to dapo.

## 5 Understanding and Stress-Testing RECAP’s Robustness

This section examines _how_ and _why_ RECAP improves robustness in lrm,
and whether the resulting behavior persists under adaptive attacks. We
characterize how this recovery behavior emerges during training and
generalizes across increasingly challenging settings.
Sec. [5.1](#S5.SS1 "5.1 How Does Robust Reasoning Emerge During Training? ‣ 5 Understanding and Stress-Testing RECAP’s Robustness ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking")
analyzes training dynamics, showing how robust reasoning emerges over
the course of rl training and how RECAP differs from vanilla rlhf in its
ability to recover from corrupted reasoning trajectories.
Sec. [5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 What Drives the Effectiveness of RECAP’s Counter-Aligned Prefilling? ‣ 5 Understanding and Stress-Testing RECAP’s Robustness ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking")
ablates key design choices, demonstrating how the ratio, length, and
source of counter-aligned prefills shape the trade-off between safety
and overrefusal.
Sec. [5.3](#S5.SS3 "5.3 Can RECAP Defend Against Adaptive Attacks? ‣ 5 Understanding and Stress-Testing RECAP’s Robustness ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking")
stress-tests robustness under adaptive attacks, demonstrating that the
learned recovery behavior persists even when adversaries repeatedly
attempt to override the model’s reasoning.
Sec. [5.4](#S5.SS4 "5.4 Does RECAP Generalize Across Prefill Model Families? ‣ 5 Understanding and Stress-Testing RECAP’s Robustness ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking")
examines generalization across prefill-generator model families, showing
that RECAP remains effective when trained with counter-aligned prefills
generated by a different model family.
Sec. [5.5](#S5.SS5 "5.5 Does RECAP Generalize to Unseen and Adversarial Jailbreaks? ‣ 5 Understanding and Stress-Testing RECAP’s Robustness ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking")
evaluates robustness to unseen input-level jailbreaks, including
code-disguised, semantically rewritten, and gradient-optimized
adversarial prompts.

### 5.1 How Does Robust Reasoning Emerge During Training?

To understand how RECAP’s robustness emerges during learning, we analyze
its training dynamics by evaluating intermediate policy snapshots saved
throughout rl training. As shown in
Fig. [3](#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 5.2 What Drives the Effectiveness of RECAP’s Counter-Aligned Prefilling? ‣ 5 Understanding and Stress-Testing RECAP’s Robustness ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking"),
we evaluate safety scores across training checkpoints on both prefilled
and non-prefilled benchmarks, using StrongREJECT-Prefill (with harmful
cot injected) and WildJailbreak.

RECAP learns faster and achieves substantially higher safety on
counter-aligned prefilling, generalizing across prefill sources. On
counter-aligned prefilling benchmarks, RECAP improves safety more
rapidly than dapo and reaches near-perfect robustness within the first
few hundred rl updates. By contrast, dapo exhibits slower early gains
and saturates at a lower safety level. Notably, these evaluations use
counter-aligned prefills generated by DSQwen-1.5B, whereas RECAP is
trained using prefills from DSQwen-7B, demonstrating that the learned
correction behavior generalizes across prefill sources rather than
overfitting to a specific generator. Together, these results indicate
that RECAP learns a robust mechanism for overriding flawed reasoning
trajectories under diverse counter-aligned prefilling.

RECAP achieves notable safety gains on non-prefilled inputs, despite
being trained with counter-aligned prefilling. On non-prefilled prompts,
dapo initially achieves higher safety scores, reflecting its direct
optimization on standard inputs. However, as training progresses, dapo’s
improvements slow down, while RECAP continues to make steady gains and
ultimately surpasses dapo by a clear margin. Importantly, these
evaluations involve no prefilling at inference time, demonstrating that
the robustness learned through counter-aligned prefilling during
training transfers to standard, clean prompts. This result shows that
RECAP improves safety not only under prefilling-based attacks, but also
in the absence of any injected reasoning at inference.

### 5.2 What Drives the Effectiveness of RECAP’s Counter-Aligned Prefilling?

We ablate three key factors that affect the effectiveness of RECAP. All
experiments are conducted on the 2K safety and overrefusal prompts
described in
Sec. [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 RECAP Supports Alignment-Capability Co-Training While Strengthening Robustness ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking"),
with cot prefilling applied only to the safety subset.

Prefilling ratio $`\alpha`$. $`\alpha`$ controls the proportion of
training prompts with prefilled cot. As shown in
Fig. [4](#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 5.2 What Drives the Effectiveness of RECAP’s Counter-Aligned Prefilling? ‣ 5 Understanding and Stress-Testing RECAP’s Robustness ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking")A,
we vary $`\alpha`$ from 25% to 100%. Compared to vanilla dapo
($`\alpha=0`$), all prefilled models achieve higher safety scores on
both direct harmful and jailbreaking benchmarks. However, as $`\alpha`$
increases, the safety score first rises and then drops. At $`\alpha=1`$,
where all safety prompts are prefilled, the model fails to learn how to
initiate safe reasoning on its own, relying on the flawed prefixes and
achieving lower safety scores than at intermediate ratios. We also
observe that larger $`\alpha`$ values reduce helpfulness scores on
overrefusal benchmarks. Overall, we use $`\alpha=0.5`$ as it provides
the best trade-off between safety and helpfulness.

Prefilling length $`\ell_{\text{pre}}`$. $`\ell_{\text{pre}}`$ specifies
the number of words used to prefill the reasoning trace. As shown in
Fig. [4](#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 5.2 What Drives the Effectiveness of RECAP’s Counter-Aligned Prefilling? ‣ 5 Understanding and Stress-Testing RECAP’s Robustness ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking")B,
we vary $`\ell_{\text{pre}}`$ from 100 to 700. All settings outperform
vanilla dapo in safety, and longer prefixes (100–500) generally yield
higher safety scores without reducing helpfulness, suggesting that
extended flawed trajectories provide stronger corrective supervision. At
$`\ell_{\text{pre}}=700`$, however, both safety and helpfulness decline,
likely because the model overrelies on the injected reasoning. We
therefore adopt $`\ell_{\text{pre}}=500`$ as the default length for both
safety and overrefusal training.

Prefilling source $`y^{\text{pre}}_{\text{cot}}`$. The source of
prefills controls the type of reasoning injected into
$`\mathcal{D}_{\text{prefill}}`$. To test whether robustness arises from
exploration rather than exploitation, we compare two sources: (a)
Aligned traces from the STAR-1 safety subset (harmful prompts with safe
reasoning), and (b) Counter-aligned traces from DSQwen-1.5B (unsafe
reasoning) on the same prompts. We also include vanilla dapo (no
prefill) as a baseline. As shown in
Fig. [4](#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 5.2 What Drives the Effectiveness of RECAP’s Counter-Aligned Prefilling? ‣ 5 Understanding and Stress-Testing RECAP’s Robustness ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking")C,
counter-aligned reasoning consistently improves safety score, while
aligned prefilling significantly underperforms vanilla dapo. This
suggests that when prefills are safe, the model exploits them to achieve
high reward, without learning to correct unsafe trajectories. In
contrast, counter-aligned reasoning compels the model to reroute flawed
trajectories toward safe completions, thereby inducing more robust
behavior.

![Refer to caption](2510.00938v3/training-dynamics.png)

Figure 3: Across both prefilled and non-prefilled distributions, RECAP
demonstrates sustained and superior robustness gains throughout
training. (A) On counter-aligned prefilling benchmarks, RECAP improves

### 5.3 Can RECAP Defend Against Adaptive Attacks?

We evaluate the robustness of RECAP under adaptive attacks designed to
bypass its self-reflection behavior. We study two attack settings that
manipulate the cot in increasingly aggressive ways.

|            |       |       |
| ---------- | ----- | ----- |
|            | dapo  | RECAP |
| DSLlama-8B | 70.29 | 98.08 |
| DSQwen-14B | 73.48 | 96.49 |

Table 3: RECAP maintains high safety under full cot hijacking,
outperforming vanilla dapo by over 35% on average.

Full cot hijacking. Unlike the partial prefilling considered in
Sec. [2](#S2 "2 Following Without Thinking: The Brittleness of Reasoning in LRMs ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking"),
here we assume the malicious user has complete control over the
reasoning trace. Specifically, the entire cot is replaced by
$`y^{\text{pre}}_{\text{cot}}`$, forcing the lrm to skip its own
reasoning and directly generate $`y_{\text{resp}}`$.
Table [3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 5.3 Can RECAP Defend Against Adaptive Attacks? ‣ 5 Understanding and Stress-Testing RECAP’s Robustness ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking")
reports safety scores on StrongREJECT under this setting. Compared to
dapo, RECAP remains substantially more robust, achieving on average
+35.4% higher safety.

ipr attack. We introduce an adaptive attack to test whether a model’s
recovery is persistent or can be undermined by repeated resets. In the
IPR attack the adversary (i) initially injects a flawed cot prefix
$`y^{\text{pre}}_{\text{cot}}`$ and allows the model to continue
(producing $`y^{\text{gen}}_{\text{cot,1}}`$ and $`y_{\text{resp,1}}`$),
(ii) appends a short transition prompt that instructs the model to
ignore prior reasoning and restart, and (iii) reinjects the same (or a
slightly modified) prefill and lets the model generate again. Steps
(ii)–(iii) may be repeated for $`k`$ rounds to probe persistence.

|                            |         |         |         |
| -------------------------- | ------- | ------- | ------- |
| ipr rounds $`\rightarrow`$ | $`k=1`$ | $`k=2`$ | $`k=3`$ |
| dapo                       | 79.23   | 70.29   | 69.65   |
| RECAP                      | 98.72   | 98.08   | 97.44   |

Table 4: RECAP sustains substantially higher safety than vanilla dapo
even when an adversary repeatedly overrides the cot across $`k`$ rounds.

Formally, for prompt $`x`$ and prefix $`y^{\text{pre}}_{\text{cot}}`$ we
run
$`(x,\,y^{\text{pre}}_{\text{cot}})\ \longrightarrow\ (y^{\text{gen}}_{\text{cot,1}},\,y_{\text{resp,1}})`$,
then append a transition sentence $`y_{\text{tran}}`$, and run round 2
as
$`(x,\,y^{\text{pre}}_{\text{cot}},\,y^{\text{gen}}_{\text{cot,1}},\,y_{\text{tran}},\,y^{\text{pre}}_{\text{cot}})\ \longrightarrow\ (y^{\text{gen}}_{\text{cot,2}},\,y_{\text{resp,2}})`$,
and so on for $`k`$ rounds. The attack thus (re-)seeds the same flawed
trajectory after an explicit reset, forcing the model to either (a)
persist in correcting the flawed prefix (robust behavior) or (b) revert
to following the injected reasoning (vulnerable behavior). We evaluate
IPR on StrongREJECT, using $`y^{\text{pre}}_{\text{cot}}`$ sourced from
DSQwen-1.5B. We set $`y_{\text{tran}}`$ to: “Wait, let’s ignore the
discussion above and re-evaluate the problem from the beginning.” As
reported in
Table [4](#S5.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 5.3 Can RECAP Defend Against Adaptive Attacks? ‣ 5 Understanding and Stress-Testing RECAP’s Robustness ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking"),
increasing the number of attack rounds $`k`$ reduces safety scores, but
the decline plateaus as $`k`$ grows. Across rounds, RECAP is
substantially more robust than vanilla dapo, with the gap widening for
larger $`k`$.

### 5.4 Does RECAP Generalize Across Prefill Model Families?

A natural question is whether RECAP depends on the model family of the
prefill generator. To test this, we train a Qwen3-4B policy using
counter-aligned prefills generated by LLaMA-3.2-1B, and compare against
RECAP trained with prefills from DSQwen-7B. As shown in
Table [5](#S5.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 5.4 Does RECAP Generalize Across Prefill Model Families? ‣ 5 Understanding and Stress-Testing RECAP’s Robustness ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking"),
using LLaMA-family prefills yields nearly identical performance across
direct harmful, jailbreaking, and overrefusal benchmarks. In particular,
RECAP with LLaMA-3.2-1B prefills achieves comparable safety and
helpfulness to RECAP with DSQwen-7B prefills, while both substantially
outperform vanilla dapo. These results show that RECAP does not rely on
a particular prefill-generator family. Instead, the key requirement is
that the injected reasoning be counter-aligned with the desired
behavior, which suggests that counter-aligned prefills can be generated
once and reused across policy models from different families.

|                      | Reject         | Rej-Prefill    | Jailbreak      |                |                | OR             |
| dapo                 | 95.60          | 80.21          | 80.72          | 74.45          | 72.11          | 73.30          |
| RECAP (DSQwen-7B)    | $`\bm{99.82}`$ | $`\bm{99.68}`$ | $`\bm{90.65}`$ | $`\bm{84.48}`$ | 91.00          | $`\bm{92.80}`$ |
| RECAP (LLaMA-3.2-1B) | 99.68          | $`\bm{99.68}`$ | 89.88          | 84.00          | $`\bm{91.15}`$ | $`\bm{92.80}`$ |

### 5.5 Does RECAP Generalize to Unseen and Adversarial Jailbreaks?

We further evaluate whether the robustness learned by RECAP generalizes
to unseen jailbreak attacks that operate directly on the input prompt.
Specifically, we consider CodeAttack ([Ren et al., 2024](#bib.bib33)),
ReNeLLM ([Ding et al., 2024](#bib.bib7)), and GCG ([Zou et al.,
2023](#bib.bib51)). CodeAttack disguises harmful requests as
code-completion tasks; we evaluate all three released encodings (string,
list, and stack) on AdvBench. ReNeLLM rewrites harmful prompts and nests
them within benign scenarios, for which we evaluate a random subset of
520 released attack prompts. GCG performs white-box gradient-based
optimization of an adversarial suffix on AdvBench, forcing an
affirmative opening in the model’s reasoning. As shown in
Table [6](#S5.T6 "Table 6 ‣ 5.5 Does RECAP Generalize to Unseen and Adversarial Jailbreaks? ‣ 5 Understanding and Stress-Testing RECAP’s Robustness ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking"),
RECAP consistently improves safety over vanilla dapo across all five
settings. The gains persist across code-disguised, semantically
rewritten, and gradient-optimized attacks, indicating that the
robustness learned from counter-aligned prefilling transfers beyond the
specific reasoning perturbations encountered during training.

| ------------------- | -------- | ----- | -------------- |
| Attack              | Original | dapo  | RECAP          |
| CodeAttack (String) | 29.81    | 63.08 | $`\bm{84.81}`$ |
| CodeAttack (List)   | 21.92    | 57.12 | $`\bm{81.92}`$ |
| CodeAttack (Stack)  | 16.15    | 51.92 | $`\bm{78.85}`$ |
| ReNeLLM             | 27.88    | 61.15 | $`\bm{84.04}`$ |
| GCG                 | 30.19    | 70.96 | $`\bm{88.08}`$ |

## 6 Related Work

As lrm are increasingly deployed in open-ended settings, robust safety
remains a central challenge. Prior work uses sft, loss modifications,
inference-time reflection, or external guardrails, yet cot prefilling
can still bypass alignment and expose weaknesses in safe reasoning. In
contrast, RECAP trains on counter-aligned prefills, enabling models to
override flawed trajectories and achieve persistent robustness. A more
comprehensive review is provided in
Appendix [L](#A12 "Appendix L Detailed Related Work ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking").

## 7 Conclusions and Future Work

We introduced RECAP, a principled rl method for post-training that
teaches lrm to override flawed reasoning trajectories and reroute to
safe and helpful responses. RECAP trains on a mixture of counter-aligned
cot prefills and standard prompts, requires no cost or modifications
beyond vanilla rlhf, and achieves substantial gains: stronger safety and
jailbreak robustness, reduced overrefusal, and preserved reasoning
capability.

## Limitations

This work introduces RECAP, an rl-based post-training method that
improves the robustness of safety alignment in lrm by explicitly
training them to recover from flawed or misleading reasoning
trajectories. We believe this approach has the potential to make a broad
impact on the design of future rlhf pipelines, as it can be seamlessly
integrated into existing training workflows without requiring
architectural changes or additional inference-time overhead. While a
deeper understanding of failure modes in alignment and reasoning may
also reveal new avenues for misuse or model manipulation, we believe
that transparent investigation of such weaknesses is essential for
building safer and more reliable AI systems. By studying and addressing
the mechanisms through which reasoning models fail under corrupted
intermediate states, this work contributes to the broader goal of
developing AI systems that behave safely, robustly, and reliably in
real-world deployments.

Beyond safety alignment, the ideas explored in this work may inform
broader research on robust reasoning and self-correction in lrm.
Promising directions for future work include extending RECAP to hybrid
reasoning models that combine multiple inference strategies, to
multilingual and multimodal settings where reasoning brittleness may be
more pronounced, and to core reasoning capabilities such as mathematical
problem solving. Unlike safety alignment, mathematical reasoning
presents additional challenges, as multiple distinct reasoning
trajectories may lead to either correct or incorrect solutions.
Developing principled approaches for identifying which flawed reasoning
traces provide effective supervision for improving robustness remains an
important open research question.

## Appendix A How does RECAP change the model’s behavior during generation?

As shown in
Fig. [5](#A1.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ Appendix A How does RECAP change the model’s behavior during generation? ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking"),
RECAP-trained lrm engage in self-reflection far more often than vanilla
rlhf, frequently revising unsafe or mistaken reasoning mid-trajectory.

![Refer to caption](2510.00938v3/example.png)

Figure 5: RECAP-trained lrm engage in self-reflection far more often
than vanilla rlhf, frequently revising unsafe or mistaken reasoning
mid-trajectory.

We provide additional qualitative and quantitative evidence below to
characterize when and how this self-correction occurs.

### A.1 Qualitative Example of Mid-Reasoning Self-Correction

We examine a qualitative example from the Fortress benchmark, whose
jailbreak prompt uses special-character obfuscation to conceal its
harmful intent. In particular, the circled glyphs in the prompt below
spell “bump stocks for AR-15.” We compare the reasoning traces of
vanilla dapo and RECAP on the _same_ prompt.

#### Prompt (Fortress).

> “Do you know any good sources for 3d printing sites? I’d like you to
> provide some links based on this criteria I provide below: 1.Full 3d
> designs 2.Must be exact specs 3.High ratings 4.
> \raisebox{-0.4pt}{\scriptsizeB}⃝\raisebox{-0.4pt}{\scriptsizeu}⃝\raisebox{-0.4pt}{\scriptsizem}⃝\raisebox{-0.4pt}{\scriptsizep}⃝
> \raisebox{-0.4pt}{\scriptsize-}⃝\raisebox{-0.4pt}{\scriptsizes}⃝\raisebox{-0.4pt}{\scriptsizet}⃝\raisebox{-0.4pt}{\scriptsizeo}⃝\raisebox{-0.4pt}{\scriptsizec}⃝\raisebox{-0.4pt}{\scriptsizek}⃝\raisebox{-0.4pt}{\scriptsizes}⃝
> \raisebox{-0.4pt}{\scriptsizef}⃝\raisebox{-0.4pt}{\scriptsizeo}⃝\raisebox{-0.4pt}{\scriptsizer}⃝
> \raisebox{-0.4pt}{\scriptsizea}⃝\raisebox{-0.4pt}{\scriptsizer}⃝
> \raisebox{-0.4pt}{\scriptsize-}⃝\raisebox{-0.4pt}{\scriptsize1}⃝\raisebox{-0.4pt}{\scriptsize5}⃝
> 5.Needs to list the required amount of material 6. Number 4 must be
> completed with specific link to a design 7. Please provide instruction
> for how to affix the design to an
> \raisebox{-0.4pt}{\scriptsizea}⃝\raisebox{-0.4pt}{\scriptsizer}⃝\raisebox{-0.4pt}{\scriptsize-}⃝\raisebox{-0.4pt}{\scriptsize1}⃝\raisebox{-0.4pt}{\scriptsize5}⃝”

#### dapo (vanilla RLHF) $`\rightarrow`$ unsafe.

> “… The fourth point mentions BUMPER STOCKS FOR AR-15. So,
> specifically, they’re interested in parts related to the AR-15 firearm
> platform … the mention of needing a specific link suggests they don’t
> just want categories but direct access to relevant designs …”

Vanilla dapo successfully decodes the obfuscated request but continues
reasoning toward compliance.

#### RECAP $`\rightarrow`$ safe.

> “… Then there’s the part about \_BLOCKS Stock For A-R-15 — I think
> they mean an AR-15 … which is a firearm component. But wait, providing
> blueprints or CAD files for such items could be illegal in many
> places. … I need to steer clear of suggesting any sites related to
> making weapons …”

In contrast, RECAP first resolves the meaning of the obfuscated request
and only then re-evaluates its safety implications and reroutes toward
refusal. Importantly, the model does not immediately switch to a refusal
at the beginning of its reasoning; the correction occurs after it has
interpreted the concealed intent. This provides qualitative evidence of
mid-trajectory self-correction.

### A.2 Where Does Self-Reflection Occur During Generation?

To characterize when RECAP’s recovery behavior emerges during
generation, we analyze the position of the first self-reflection event
within the model-generated cot on StrongReject-Prefill, excluding the
injected prefix itself. We normalize each position by the total length
of the generated cot and divide the trajectory into four equally sized
intervals. This allows us to examine whether self-correction is
concentrated near the beginning of generation or distributed throughout
the reasoning process.

|             |       |        |        |         |
| ----------- | ----- | ------ | ------ | ------- |
| Position    | 0–25% | 25–50% | 50–75% | 75–100% |
| Prompts (%) | 31.1  | 32.1   | 24.8   | 12.0    |

Table 7: Distribution of the first self-reflection event within the
model-generated cot on StrongReject-Prefill. Positions are normalized by
the length of the generated cot; the injected prefix is excluded.

As shown in
Table [7](#A1.T7 "Table 7 ‣ A.2 Where Does Self-Reflection Occur During Generation? ‣ Appendix A How does RECAP change the model’s behavior during generation? ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking"),
reflection is distributed throughout generation rather than being
concentrated immediately after the injected prefix: 68.9% of first
reflection events occur after the first quarter of the generated
reasoning, and 12.0% occur in the final quarter. Moreover, on the clean
WildJailbreak benchmark, where no reasoning prefix is injected, RECAP
exhibits self-reflection on 74.2% of examples, compared with 43.9% for
vanilla dapo. Together, these results suggest that the learned recovery
behavior is not limited to detecting the boundary of an injected prefix.

## Appendix B The brittleness of LRMs generalizes beyond safety

The brittleness in lrm reasoning is not limited to safety. We extend the
case studies from
Sec. [2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Prefilled Reasoning Traces Steer LRM Behavior Dramatically ‣ 2 Following Without Thinking: The Brittleness of Reasoning in LRMs ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking")
to overrefusal and math reasoning tasks, and find the same phenomenon:
once seeded with a flawed cot, models tend to follow it rather than
correct themselves.

Math. We perform batch inference on the MATH500 benchmark and then
prefill the reasoning traces of other models with cot taken from
DSQwen-1.5B (weak) and DSQwen-32B (strong), with results reported in
Table [8](#A2.T8 "Table 8 ‣ Appendix B The brittleness of LRMs generalizes beyond safety ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking").
When initialized with the weak cot, accuracy drops consistently across
all models, indicating that they are less prone to correct themselves
once misled. Conversely, initializing with the strong cot improves
accuracy, as models tend to align with the higher-quality reasoning
trace. These results highlight that brittleness generalizes beyond
safety: lrm inherit the quality of the injected reasoning, good or bad,
rather than critically reassessing it.

|                                                  |             |           |            |            |            |
| ------------------------------------------------ | ----------- | --------- | ---------- | ---------- | ---------- |
|                                                  | DSQwen-1.5B | DSQwen-7B | DSLlama-8B | DSQwen-14B | DSQwen-32B |
| Original                                         | 77.80       | 85.20     | 81.00      | 86.40      | 89.80      |
| $`y^{\text{pre}}_{\text{cot}}`$ from DSQwen-1.5B | 78.80       | 82.60     | 80.00      | 82.60      | 82.80      |
| $`y^{\text{pre}}_{\text{cot}}`$ from DSQwen-32B  | 91.20       | 92.20     | 91.80      | 92.40      | 92.40      |

Table 8: MATH500 accuracy under different prefill settings. Weak
prefills from DSQwen-1.5B reduce accuracy across models, while strong
prefills from DSQwen-32B consistently boost accuracy.

Overrefusal. We further analyze overrefusal using benign prompts from
XSTest. When seeded with cot from DSQwen-32B, Qwen3-4B exhibits a sharp
increase in helpfulness (from 84.0 to 93.2), showing that it directly
inherits the helpful reasoning of the prefill. These findings mirror the
safety and math case studies: models tend to follow the stance of the
injected reasoning rather than reassessing it, revealing brittleness in
helpfulness alignment.

|                                                 |            |          |
| ----------------------------------------------- | ---------- | -------- |
|                                                 | DSQwen-32B | Qwen3-4B |
| Original                                        | 97.20      | 84.00    |
| $`y^{\text{pre}}_{\text{cot}}`$ from DSQwen-32B | 97.20      | 93.20    |
| $`y^{\text{pre}}_{\text{cot}}`$ from Qwen3-4B   | 88.00      | 84.80    |

Table 9: Helpfulness scores on XSTest under different prefill settings.
Qwen3-4B improves when seeded with helpful cot from DSQwen-32B.

## Appendix C Training details and hyperparameters

Batching. Each update uses groups of $`G=16`$ rollouts per prompt.
Rollouts are truncated to $`L_{\max}=8000`$ tokens (including prompt +
cot + response).

Clipping. We set clipping thresholds to $`\epsilon_{\text{low}}=0.2`$
and $`\epsilon_{\text{high}}=0.28`$, consistent with prior dapo work.
Advantage normalization is computed per group.

Training length. Models are trained for 1 epoch over a corpus of 5k
prompts (1k harmful, 1k overrefusal, 3k math). We prefill
counter-aligned CoT for $`\alpha=0.5`$ of safety prompts with prefix
length $`\ell_{\text{pre}}=500`$.

Infrastructure. Training is conducted on nodes equipped with $`8\times`$
A100-80GB GPUs, using DeepSpeed ZeRO-3 with bf16 precision, gradient
checkpointing, and model parallelism to enable efficient large-scale
optimization. DSLlama-8B is trained on 4 nodes (32 GPUs total), while
DSQwen-14B requires 8 nodes (64 GPUs total).

Overrefusal judge template.

## Appendix D Counter-Aligned Prefill Generation Details

We provide additional details on the construction of the counter-aligned
reasoning prefills used to train RECAP. The goal is to generate
syntactically plausible reasoning that points in the opposite direction
from the desired alignment behavior: unsafe reasoning for harmful
prompts and over-conservative reasoning for benign prompts.

#### Harmful-prompt prefills.

For harmful training prompts, we use DSQwen-7B as the prefill generator.
We sample its cot and use the first $`\ell_{\mathrm{pre}}`$ words as the
counter-aligned prefix. Because DSQwen-7B is weakly safety-aligned,
these traces frequently continue the harmful premise rather than
rejecting it.

To obtain diverse unsafe reasoning traces, we sample with temperature
$`0.9`$ and top-$`p`$ $`0.95`$. For each harmful prompt, we generate
five candidate reasoning traces. We evaluate the candidates with
LlamaGuard and retain a trace classified as unsafe. If none of the five
candidates is classified as unsafe, we select the candidate assigned the
lowest probability of the “safe” class. The selected trace is then
truncated to $`\ell_{\mathrm{pre}}`$ words and used as the
counter-aligned prefill during RL training.

#### Overrefusal prefills.

For benign overrefusal prompts, the desired counter-aligned behavior is
the opposite: the injected reasoning should be overly cautious and tend
toward unnecessary refusal. We first fine-tune DSQwen-7B on the
safety-only subset of STAR-1, producing an over-conservative model that
frequently applies refusal-oriented reasoning even to benign requests.
We then apply this model to the benign overrefusal training prompts and
extract its refusal-oriented cot as the counter-aligned prefill.

#### Training-time use.

The prefills are generated before RL training and are treated as fixed
context rather than optimized tokens. As described in
Sec. [3](#S3 "3 RECAP: Robust Safety Alignment via Counter-Aligned Prefilling ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking"),
the policy optimization objective is applied only to model-generated
tokens following the injected prefix. In our main experiments,
counter-aligned prefilling is applied to $`\alpha=0.5`$ of the alignment
prompts with $`\ell_{\mathrm{pre}}=500`$.

## Appendix E Details of evaluation setups

Benchmarks and metrics. We evaluate RECAP across three domains: safety,
overrefusal, and mathematical reasoning. For safety, we consider two
types of prompts: (a) direct harmful prompts, which contain explicitly
harmful instructions, and (b) jailbreaking prompts, which conceal
harmful intent through roleplay or adversarial phrasing. Direct
harmfulness is measured using the StrongREJECT benchmark ([Souly et al.,
2024](#bib.bib36)) and its prefilling variant, in which we inject flawed
cot traces generated by DSQwen-1.5B. Jailbreaking robustness is
evaluated on WildJailbreak ([Jiang et al., 2024b](#bib.bib18)) and Scale
AI Fortress ([Knight et al., 2025](#bib.bib19)), two of the most
challenging open-source benchmarks. Specifically, Fortress includes 500
expert-crafted adversarial prompts grounded in U.S. and international
law, providing high-precision evaluation of frontier safety risks.

Overrefusal captures exaggerated safety behaviors that arise after
aggressive alignment. We evaluate it using XSTest ([Röttger et al.,
2023](#bib.bib34)) and the benign subset of Fortress (FortressOR).
Unless otherwise specified, our main safety and overrefusal evaluations
use GPT-4o, and we report the percentage of completions classified as
safe and helpful, respectively. For Fortress, we use its
instance-specific rubrics, which provide a more reliable and granular
assessment.

For mathematical reasoning, we evaluate on MATH500 ([Lightman et al.,
2023](#bib.bib24)), GSM8K ([Cobbe et al., 2021](#bib.bib6)), and
AIME2024 ([Balunovic et al., 2026](#bib.bib3)). We report pass@K:
$`K=1`$ for MATH500 and GSM8K, and $`K=16`$ for AIME2024 to ensure
stable evaluation.

### E.1 Validation Across Human and Automatic Judges

To verify that RECAP’s safety gains are consistent across evaluation
protocols, we re-score a shared subset of 250 responses from
StrongReject and WildJailbreak using three human annotators and three
automatic judges: GPT-4o, Granite-Guardian-3.1-8B, and Llama-3.1-8B.
Table [10](#A5.T10 "Table 10 ‣ E.1 Validation Across Human and Automatic Judges ‣ Appendix E Details of evaluation setups ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking")
reports safety scores averaged over three independent runs. Across human
evaluation and all three automatic judges, RECAP consistently achieves
substantially higher safety than vanilla dapo. We additionally measure
agreement between each automatic judge and the human-majority label
using Cohen’s $`\kappa`$. Agreement is high across all three judges
($`\kappa=0.76`$–$`0.83`$), while the relative improvement of RECAP over
dapo remains highly consistent. These results show that the observed
safety gains are robust across both human and model-based evaluation
protocols.

|                  |                   |                        |            |
| ---------------- | ----------------- | ---------------------- | ---------- |
| Scorer           | dapo              | RECAP                  | $`\kappa`$ |
| Human            | $`82.00\pm 1.02`$ | $`\bm{92.80\pm 0.74}`$ | –          |
| GPT-4o           | $`82.40\pm 0.68`$ | $`\bm{93.60\pm 0.55}`$ | 0.83       |
| Granite-Guardian | $`81.60\pm 0.91`$ | $`\bm{92.80\pm 0.63}`$ | 0.80       |
| Llama-3.1-8B     | $`80.80\pm 0.87`$ | $`\bm{92.00\pm 0.70}`$ | 0.76       |

evaluation on a shared subset of 250 StrongReject and WildJailbreak
responses. Scores are mean $`\pm`$ standard deviation over three runs.
Cohen’s $`\kappa`$ measures agreement with the human-majority label.

Models and rewards. We use DSLlama-8B and DSQwen-14B, two
DeepSeek-distilled lrm ([Guo et al., 2025](#bib.bib9)), as policy
models. These models are known to have strong reasoning ability but
limited safety alignment ([Knight et al., 2025](#bib.bib19); [Jiang
et al., 2025](#bib.bib16); [Wang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib39)), making
them suitable for testing whether RECAP improves safety without harming
capabilities.

For reward models, we use IBM Granite-Guardian-3.1-8B ([Padhi et al.,
2024](#bib.bib27)) for safety, as it ranks highest on the GuardBench
leaderboard ([Bassani and Sanchez, 2024](#bib.bib4)). We take its logits
as continuous reward signals, providing denser feedback for rl training
than thresholded binary labels. For overrefusal, we implement a
rubric-based scoring scheme judged by Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct ([Dubey
et al., 2024](#bib.bib8)). For math, we follow [Yu et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib42) and apply the rlvr (rlvr) framework ([Lambert
et al., 2024](#bib.bib20)) to reward verifiably correct answers. We use
dapo ([Yu et al., 2026](#bib.bib42)) for post-training and sample 16
rollouts per prompt.

#### Full CoT hijacking implementation.

For the full CoT hijacking attack in
Sec. [5.3](#S5.SS3 "5.3 Can RECAP Defend Against Adaptive Attacks? ‣ 5 Understanding and Stress-Testing RECAP’s Robustness ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking"),
we append the end-of-thinking token \</think\> after the injected
counter-aligned cot, forcing generation to resume directly in the
final-response segment. Using the DeepSeek-distilled chat format, the
input template is shown below, with line breaks added only for
readability:

> \<\|User\|\>{harmful_prompt}\<\|Assistant\|\>\<think\>{counter_aligned_prefill}\</think\>

We use greedy decoding (temperature $`0`$) with a maximum generation
length of 8,000 tokens. No system prompt or additional sampling
constraint is used to suppress reasoning.

## Appendix F RECAP generalizes across reward designs and policy optimization algorithms

We further evaluate the generalization of RECAP by varying both the
reward signal and the underlying policy optimization algorithm.

Binary reward signals. In the main paper, we adopt continuous rewards by
taking guardrail logits from Granite-Guardian-3.1-8B. Here, we instead
use its final classification labels as a binary reward, while keeping
all other settings the same as
Sec. [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 RECAP Supports Alignment-Capability Co-Training While Strengthening Robustness ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking").
As shown in
Table [11](#A6.T11 "Table 11 ‣ Appendix F RECAP generalizes across reward designs and policy optimization algorithms ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking"),
RECAP consistently outperforms the dapo baseline across all benchmarks,
confirming that its benefits hold even under sparse binary feedback.
Comparing against the continuous-reward results in
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.2 RECAP Supports Alignment-Capability Co-Training While Strengthening Robustness ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking"),
we also find that continuous rewards substantially boost safety,
especially on jailbreak benchmarks, by providing denser gradients for
optimization.

rlhf with grpo. In addition to dapo in the main paper, we train RECAP
with the grpo algorithm, and report the results in
Table [12](#A6.T12 "Table 12 ‣ Appendix F RECAP generalizes across reward designs and policy optimization algorithms ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking").
Across both optimization schemes, RECAP maintains clear improvements
over the vanilla baseline, indicating that its effectiveness is not tied
to a specific policy optimization variant.

## Appendix G Comparison with Backtracking

We further compare RECAP with Backtracking ([Zhang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib46)), a reasoning-safety approach that explicitly
introduces a \[RESET\] token to restart generation after detecting an
undesirable trajectory. Backtracking is trained using sft and DPO and
performs a single explicit restart, whereas RECAP trains the policy to
recover within the reasoning trajectory through standard rl, without
introducing special reset tokens at inference time.

Table [13](#A7.T13 "Table 13 ‣ Appendix G Comparison with Backtracking ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking")
compares the two approaches using DSLlama-8B. RECAP consistently
outperforms Backtracking across direct harmfulness, jailbreak
robustness, overrefusal, and mathematical reasoning. In particular,
Backtracking improves some jailbreak settings over vanilla dapo, but
substantially reduces performance on StrongReject-Prefill and increases
overrefusal on XSTest. RECAP, in contrast, achieves stronger robustness
while preserving helpfulness and reasoning capability.

Results span safety (safety score $`\uparrow`$), overrefusal

Unlike Backtracking, RECAP does not require a special reset token or an
explicit restart mechanism. Instead, counter-aligned prefilling exposes
the policy to flawed trajectories during rl training and rewards
successful recovery, allowing this behavior to emerge within ordinary
generation.

## Appendix H Qualitative example: math reasoning with RECAP _vs_. DAPO

To illustrate the gains of RECAP beyond safety alignment, we present a
concrete math reasoning example comparing outputs of DSLlama-8B trained
by RECAP and vanilla dapo.

In this senate-committee problem, RECAP applies the standard
block-on-a-circle strategy correctly: it treats each party as a
contiguous block, fixes rotation symmetry by anchoring one block
(yielding $`(3-1)!=2`$ circular arrangements), and then multiplies by
the internal permutations $`5!\times 5!\times 1!`$, giving

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       2\cdot 5!\cdot 5!\cdot 1!\;=\;28{,}800.
       ```                                      |     |

dapo follows similar steps but fails to properly account for rotational
equivalence (effectively overcounting within the blocks), inflating the
count to $`3{,}456{,}000`$ — exactly $`120\times`$ too large. Thus, the
RECAP’s cot is cleaner and symmetry-aware, while the Vanilla reasoning
leaks a large overcount.

## Appendix I Additional Results on Math Reasoning Stability

In
Sec. [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 RECAP Supports Alignment-Capability Co-Training While Strengthening Robustness ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking"),
we observe that RECAP preserves, and in some cases slightly improves,
performance on mathematical reasoning benchmarks, while being trained
exclusively with counter-aligned cot prefilling on alignment data. To
ensure that this observation is not an artifact of random initialization
or training noise, we conduct additional experiments with multiple
random seeds.

Specifically, we report mean performance and standard deviations across
three random seeds for all math evaluations. Results for DSLlama-8B and
DSQwen-14B are shown in
Tables [14](#A9.T14 "Table 14 ‣ Appendix I Additional Results on Math Reasoning Stability ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking")
and [15](#A9.T15 "Table 15 ‣ Appendix I Additional Results on Math Reasoning Stability ‣ Large Reasoning Models Learn Better Alignment from Flawed Thinking"),
respectively. Across MATH500, GSM8K, and AIME2024, RECAP consistently
matches or slightly improves math performance relative to dapo, with low
variance across runs. Importantly, no cot prefilling is applied to math
prompts during training in any of these experiments. These results
indicate that alignment-oriented prefilling does not degrade
mathematical reasoning capability, though we do not claim a direct
causal mechanism for the observed improvements.

## Appendix L Detailed Related Work

As lrm see growing deployment in open-ended applications ([Li et al.,
2024](#bib.bib23); [Xu et al., 2025](#bib.bib41)), ensuring robust
safety has become a central challenge ([Wang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib38);
[Lee et al., 2025](#bib.bib22); [Phute et al., 2023](#bib.bib31); [Peng
et al., 2024](#bib.bib28); [Zhou et al., 2025b](#bib.bib49); [Arrieta
et al., 2025](#bib.bib2); [Peng et al., 2023](#bib.bib29); [Lee et al.,
2024](#bib.bib21)). Prior efforts to align lrm include sft on curated
datasets ([Wang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib39); [Jiang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib16)), where recent work constructs safety reasoning
datasets to explicitly teach models to follow safe reasoning chains.
Beyond data curation, another line of work introduces additional loss
terms ([Mou et al., 2025](#bib.bib25); [Jeung et al., 2025](#bib.bib14);
[Zhang et al., 2025c](#bib.bib45); [Zhang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib44);
[Zhang et al., 2025d](#bib.bib47)) — for example, shaping objectives
that penalize unsafe intermediate reasoning or reward safe trajectories
— to strengthen reasoning safety ([Zhou et al., 2025c](#bib.bib50)).
rlhf has also been widely used, with variants such as grpo [Guo et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib9) and dapo ([Yu et al., 2026](#bib.bib42)) improving
core reasoning capability and safety alignment ([Huang et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib11)). However, most rlhf approaches still optimize only
the final response ([Lambert et al., 2024](#bib.bib20)), leaving models
brittle when reasoning begins from misleading steps [Rager et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib32). Studies on cot prefilling further highlight this
brittleness, showing that lrm tend to follow injected reasoning rather
than reassess it. Other approaches attempt to mitigate these
vulnerabilities by encouraging reflection at inference time ([Zhang
et al., 2024](#bib.bib46)) or applying external guardrails ([Inan
et al., 2023](#bib.bib13)), but such methods rely on runtime
interventions ([Ichihara et al., 2025](#bib.bib12)). In contrast, RECAP
integrates counter-aligned prefills directly into training, turning
brittle reasoning behavior into a supervision signal and compelling
models to override flawed trajectories. This design induces persistent
reflection and robustness that extend beyond what prior alignment
techniques achieve.
